extracted.intended_audience: general readers, performers, and students interested in sketch comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of sketch comedy as a form: how to create and perform short comedic scenes (sketches) for stage, radio, television, or film, covering typical length, performance modes, recurring-character strategies, historical roots, festivals, and related media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic form
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sketch comedy comprises a series of short, amusing scenes or vignettes, called 'sketches' or 'skits'... performed by a group of comic actors or comedians."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the core unit (sketch/skit) and that sketch comedy is typically an ensemble form made up of multiple short pieces rather than a single continuous narrative. Useful as a definitional standard when classifying a piece as sketch comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches are "commonly between one and ten minutes long."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets an expected runtime for individual sketches; longer or shorter pieces may still be sketch-like but should be judged against this common length range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance mode: improvised vs scripted
rubrics_metrics.description: The sketches "may be improvised live by the performers, developed through improvisation before public performance, or scripted and rehearsed in advance like a play."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies acceptable creation and delivery methods — pure improv, improv-developed scripted work, or fully scripted pieces — and implies different rehearsal/training expectations depending on mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble/actor makeup
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches are "performed by a group of comic actors or comedians."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes ensemble casting as typical for the form; while solo sketch performance exists in related genres, sketch comedy conventionally involves a troupe dynamic and role-switching among members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use across media and venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch comedy is used widely in "variety shows, as well as in late night talk shows and some sitcoms," and also appears on stage, radio, television and film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates contexts where sketches are commonly presented; when producing or evaluating a sketch, consider the venue/medium because pacing, production values, and expectations differ (e.g., live stage vs televised SNL-style sketches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring characters and thematic cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: While separate sketches historically have tended to be unrelated, "more recent groups have introduced overarching themes that connect the sketches within a particular show with recurring characters that return for more than one appearance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes a stylistic choice: self-contained, unrelated sketches versus shows built around recurring characters/themes. Recurring characters can create audience attachment and enable spinoffs (films, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for spinoffs and commercial extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring characters from sketch shows (e.g., Saturday Night Live) "have notably been featured in a number of spinoff films," and sketches can be adapted into sketch films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating sketches, consider character/idea longevity and adaptability — strong recurring characters can lead to wider commercial opportunities (merchandise, films, spin-off media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical roots and stylistic antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch comedy has its origins in "music hall and vaudeville," including non-dialogue sketches (Fred Karno) and early televised examples (The Milton Berle Show).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these roots informs stylistic choices (physical comedy, sight gags, timing) and helps situate a sketch within tradition (e.g., slapstick lineage vs modern surrealism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to improvisational comedy training and scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: In North America, contemporary sketch comedy is largely an outgrowth of the "improvisational comedy scene" (The Second City, Upright Citizens Brigade, The Groundlings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights common production pipelines and training grounds; suggests that strong sketch groups often have improv-based processes and institutions as part of their development and talent pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physical and visual gags / non-verbal sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical practice includes sketches "without dialogue" (Fred Karno) and physical gags such as the "pie in the face".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that non-verbal, visual, and physical comedy are legitimate and traditional sketch techniques; consider visual staging, props, and physicality when evaluating effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch films and compilation formats
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist sketch films (feature-length compilations or related sketches), with examples ranging from early influential works to recent anthology films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting sketches to film, expect different pacing and structural needs; some sketches translate to film as collections while others are expanded to support feature-length narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festivals, revues, and development venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Many sketch comedy revues appeared at events like the Edinburgh Fringe Festival; North American sketch festivals include Chicago Sketch Fest, SF Sketchfest, and the Toronto Sketch Comedy Festival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Festivals and revues are important for development, exposure, and community building. Submission length, production values, and selection criteria at festivals influence how sketches are written and staged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and subgenre variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch comedy is "now associated mostly with adult entertainment," though "certain children's television series have also used it," and the form spans many subgenres (e.g., character, slapstick, surreal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and evaluators should consider target audience and subgenre conventions (content boundaries, tone, subject matter) when judging appropriateness and effectiveness.
